answer: Priority improvements, ordered by impact: (1) Quantify the problem and the value. The problem section is well argued but entirely qualitative. Add data on the cost of suboptimal medication titration, hospitalization/fall rates tied to poorly managed symptoms, or neurologist wait times, and cite sources. Show what a clinic or payer gains per patient (e.g., fewer unnecessary visits, faster dose adjustments) so the $15-25/month price is justified by ROI rather than assumed. (2) Replace hand-waving market claims with a bottom-up model. 'Several thousand neurologists' and 'a meaningful business if a small percentage...' are not sizing. Build TAM/SAM/SOM: number of target practices x patients per practice x realistic enrollment rate x price. Reconcile this with the $50K ARR projection, which is tiny (200 patients x $20 x 12 = ~$48K) and should be framed as a first milestone, then extended to a 3-5 year trajectory with explicit assumptions on clinic acquisition, sales cycle length, and churn. (3) Resolve the reimbursement gap. The business model hinges on clinics billing under RPM codes (e.g., CPT 99453/99454/99457), yet the team admits they have not identified which apply. Research this now: determine whether a video-based, non-FDA-cleared product qualifies as a device meeting RPM requirements (many codes require an FDA-defined medical device with automatic data transmission). If it does not, the pricing logic and clinic willingness to pay change materially; say how you will adapt. (4) Be explicit about regulatory status. State whether the software is likely a medical device (SaMD), whether it would need FDA 510(k)/De Novo or can operate under wellness/clinical-decision-support exemptions, and what claims you will and will not make. Competitors with FDA clearance are a stated advantage for them; show a credible path or a defensible positioning. Also cover HIPAA, BAAs, video encryption, retention policy, and consent, which are currently only gestured at. (5) Strengthen the validation plan with a concrete design. Specify the comparator (MDS-UPDRS tremor items), target sample size, number of raters, success metrics (e.g., correlation/ICC thresholds), timeline, budget, and what happens if accuracy falls short. Also address real-world confounders: lighting, camera angle, phone stability, caregiver variability, and adherence to a daily recording habit among older users. Share any early accuracy or usability data from the pilot. (6) Use the pilot as evidence. They have a paying customer, which is their strongest asset but is described vaguely. Report number of patients, adherence rate, completion time, clinician feedback, any changes in clinical decisions, and willingness to renew or expand. Include a quote or letter of support. (7) Sharpen competition and differentiation. Build a comparison table (accuracy, cost, setup friction, FDA status, data continuity). Acknowledge the accuracy trade-off but articulate why 'good enough, universal, and cheap' wins for specific use cases, and consider whether video-based approaches or smartphone sensor apps already exist and how Tremorlog is distinct. Address defensibility: what is proprietary beyond a computer vision pipeline (data moat, clinical validation, workflow integration)? (8) Address integration and clinic workflow. Neurology practices live in EHRs; discuss how data gets into the chart, who reviews flags, and how this avoids adding clinician burden or alert fatigue. Define what a 'significant change' flag means and who is liable if one is missed. (9) Tighten go-to-market. Explain how the team will find and close clinics (sales cycle, champion, procurement hurdles, per-practice onboarding effort), and give a customer acquisition cost estimate. Include unit economics: hosting/storage per patient per month versus price, since video storage was flagged as a significant cost. (10) Fix team and structure gaps in the document, not just the roadmap. Name the neurologist advisor (with consent) and describe their commitment; clarify founder equity, vesting, and IP ownership, especially given university affiliation. Present a concrete plan and timeline for adding clinical and regulatory expertise. (11) Quality and presentation. Correct typos and grammar ('effects' vs 'affects', 'alot', 'judgement' consistency), remove placeholders like 'a student startup from our university' in favor of a one-sentence value proposition, add a funding-use table with amounts and milestones tied to measurable outcomes, a 12-18 month roadmap, and a short risk section listing top risks (accuracy, reimbursement, regulation, adherence) with mitigations. Replace vague phrases ('meaningful business', 'quite quickly') with numbers. A simple web presence and a short demo video or screenshots would also make the submission more credible.
